title: Ab actis
excerpt: Ab actis is the secretary on the board of a Dutch student association, dispuut or committee.
example: "Did you send around the minutes of the last meeting yet?" the praeses asked the ab actis.
text: The ab actis takes the minutes, handles the emails and keeps the admin of the club in order. After the praeses, they are often the first person to go to. The name is Latin and means something like "in charge of the records". Every Dutch student board has one.

title: Abbo
excerpt: Abbo is Dutch slang for a subscription. Think of a gym membership, a phone plan or a streaming service.
example: "I really need to cancel my gym abbo before the end of the month," she sighed.
text: Abbo is short for "abonnement", the Dutch word for subscription. Students use it for pretty much anything you pay for every month. A Netflix abbo. A phone abbo. Or that newspaper abbo nobody ever reads.

title: Adten
excerpt: Adten (or atten) means downing your drink in one go. It is similar to chugging and usually happens when someone uses an anytimer.
example: "You lost the bet, so now you have to adten," his housemate shouted across the room.
text: The verb comes from adtje. If someone gives you an adtje, you finish your drink in one go. No breaks. Using a straw makes it even faster, and that is called a rietadt. In English you would call it chugging.

title: Adtje des
excerpt: An adtje des is an adtje you hand out when someone wasn't paying attention or makes a silly comment.
example: "That's an adtje des," she said when he asked the same question for the third time.
text: You mostly hand out an adtje des when someone clearly wasn't listening. Like asking a question that was just answered. Or making a comment that totally misses the point. The punishment? Downing your drink.

title: Adtje herhaling
excerpt: An adtje herhaling is an adtje for repeating something that was already said. Herhaling means repeat.
example: "Adtje herhaling!" the whole group shouted when he told the same joke for the second time.
text: It looks a lot like the adtje des, but this one is all about repeating yourself. Explaining a game rule again. Sharing news everybody already heard. Say it twice and you drink.

title: Adtje kratje
excerpt: Adtje kratje, also called kratzitten, is a Dutch drinking game where you finish a whole crate of beer on your own.
example: At the borrel they challenged each other to a round of adtje kratje, everyone with their own crate.
text: Whoever empties their crate first wins. A Dutch crate has 24 small bottles, so this is one of the heaviest drinking games around. Only for experienced drinkers with a very good plan. And an empty day after.

title: Adtje solidair
excerpt: An adtje solidair is an adtje you take voluntarily to support someone else.
example: When her friend was the only one who had to adten, she joined her with an adtje solidair.
text: Most adtjes are a punishment. This one isn't. You drink along to show you are in it together. It is a small act of friendship. And a great excuse to finish your drink.

title: Adulting
excerpt: Adulting means doing grown-up things, like paying bills or calling the dentist. Usually with a big sigh.
example: "I did my taxes and folded my laundry today. Serious adulting."
text: The word is almost always used as a joke. You say it when you are proud of something totally normal. Cooking a real meal. Doing your admin. Paying rent on time. For most students adulting starts the day they move out.

title: AFK
excerpt: AFK stands for away from keyboard. It means you are not at your computer or phone for a moment.
example: "AFK for five minutes, the pizza is here."
text: AFK comes from online chats and gaming. You use it to say you are gone for a bit and won't reply. People also say it when there is no keyboard anywhere near them.

title: Afko
excerpt: Afko is short for "afkorting", the Dutch word for abbreviation. Students use a lot of them.
example: "Do you get this afko?" he asked, pointing at a group chat full of random letters.
text: Dutch student associations and student houses use so many abbreviations that even the word abbreviation got shortened. Without a good dictionary you get lost fast. Luckily you found one.

title: Afpilsen
excerpt: Afpilsen means having the very last beer (or beers) of the night before everyone goes home.
example: "Shall we just afpilsen these?" he said, grabbing the last bottles from the fridge.
text: A "pils" is a regular lager in Dutch. Afpilsen is the final round. Right before everyone heads home or goes to bed. It is the student version of last call.

title: Afstubo
excerpt: Afstubo is short for "afstudeerborrel", the drinks party you throw when you graduate.
example: After years of studying she finally threw her afstubo, with speeches and way too much beer.
text: Got your bachelor or master? Then you celebrate with friends, family and housemates at your afstubo. It is often the official goodbye to student life. Next stop: becoming an arbeider.

title: Afterparty
excerpt: An afterparty is a party that keeps going after the main party has ended.
example: "The club closed at four, so we went to an afterparty at the student house."
text: An afterparty is usually smaller and later than the main event. It can be at someone's place, in a hotel or at another bar. Whoever goes to the afterparty often pays for it the next day.

title: Airfryer
excerpt: Among Dutch students, airfryer is a joke code word for a Satisfyer Pro, a sex toy. So nobody around you knows what you are really talking about.
example: "So how do you like your new airfryer?" she asked with a big wink.
text: The code name lets you talk about it in a group without outsiders getting it. Your parents think you are discussing kitchen gadgets. Your friends know better.

title: AL
excerpt: AL stands for "aspirant-lid": someone who wants to join a Dutch student association but isn't a full member yet.
example: As an AL she first had to finish the whole introduction period before becoming a member.
text: An AL is a prospective member. They only become a real member after the introduction period, called the KMT. Until then they are on probation, more or less.

title: Algorithm
excerpt: The algorithm is the system that decides which posts and videos you see on social media.
example: "I watched one video about running and now the algorithm only shows me trainers."
text: On apps like TikTok and Instagram the algorithm picks what ends up in your feed. What you watch, like and share decides what you see next. People talk about it like it is a person they know. And honestly, it does know you pretty well.

title: All-nighter
excerpt: An all-nighter means staying up all night without sleeping, usually to study or finish something.
example: "The deadline was at nine, so we pulled an all-nighter in the library."
text: All-nighters are a student classic. Especially right before an exam or a deadline. Sadly they often backfire. After a night without sleep it is a lot harder to focus. The Dutch call staying out all night doorhalen.

title: Almanak
excerpt: An almanak is the yearbook a Dutch student association publishes every year about its members and activities.
example: This year's almanak had a whole page of photos from the introduction week.
text: It is full of photos, stories and overviews of the past year, often with a full list of members. A lot of members keep their almanakken for years. They are basically a printed core memory.

title: Alt account
excerpt: An alt account is a second social media account next to your main profile.
example: "My main account is only nice photos. The weird stuff goes on my alt."
text: Alt is short for alternative. An alt account is often private or meant for a different crowd. Unlike a burner account, an alt doesn't have to be anonymous or temporary.

title: ALV
excerpt: ALV stands for "Algemene Ledenvergadering", the general members' meeting where members of a Dutch association have their say.
example: At the ALV the members voted on the new budget of the association.
text: During the ALV the board explains what it has been doing and members vote on big decisions. Think of the budget or changes to the rules. They can take hours. Drinks afterwards are pretty much mandatory.

title: Ambu
excerpt: Ambu is Dutch slang for an ambulance, usually after a night out that got out of hand.
example: After he fell over for the third time, his friends decided to call the ambu after all.
text: You mostly hear it when someone drank way too much and needs medical help. Luckily only a tiny part of nights out end like that. If in doubt, always call. In the Netherlands that number is 112.

title: Amice
excerpt: Amice is an old-fashioned, formal way to say friend. Dutch student associations use it in speeches and letters.
example: "Amice," the praeses began his speech, "tonight we celebrate a special milestone."
text: Amice comes from Latin. Inside student associations it is used as a formal way to address someone. In speeches, official letters or during an ALV. It sounds a lot grander than "hey mate".

title: Arbeider
excerpt: Arbeider means worker. Dutch students use it for the life that waits after graduating: working full time.
example: "Next year I'll just be an arbeider too," he sighed after his very last exam.
text: An arbeider works 32 to 40 hours a week, or more. It is the phase almost every student ends up in after graduating. Interns get called arbeider too. It is said with a lot of fake pity.

title: ASAP
excerpt: ASAP stands for as soon as possible.
example: "Can you put the report in the group chat ASAP? We have to hand it in tonight."
text: You see ASAP in texts, emails and at work. Some people say it like a word, others spell it out. It quickly sounds pushy though. So don't use it for everything.

title: Assessor
excerpt: The assessor is a board member of a Dutch student association with a broad, supporting role.
example: As assessor she handled all the merch and the planning of the committees this year.
text: The job is different at every club. Merch, planning, contact with old members or guiding the first-years. The assessor also takes over tasks from other board members when things get busy.

title: Assignment
excerpt: An assignment is a task for a course, like an essay, report or presentation.
example: "I can't come to the drinks, I still have to finish my assignment."
text: An assignment can be a paper, a presentation or a set of exercises. It often counts towards your final grade. And it almost always gets finished at the very last minute.

title: Ate
excerpt: Ate means someone did something really well. An outfit, a performance or a presentation was amazing.
example: "Did you see her presentation? She ate."
text: Ate is the past tense of to eat. Someone ate it up, that's how good it was. The full version is "ate and left no crumbs". The word comes from ballroom and LGBTQ+ culture.

title: Aura
excerpt: Aura is the energy or vibe someone gives off. Do something cool and you gain aura points. Do something embarrassing and you lose them.
example: "He tripped over his own laces in front of the whole bar. Minus a thousand aura."
text: On TikTok people keep track of aura points as a joke. Staying calm when everything goes wrong earns points. Making a fool of yourself costs them. Acting cool on purpose to collect aura is called aura farming.

title: Baco
excerpt: Baco is short for Bacardi cola, a popular drink at Dutch student parties.
example: At the bar he ordered his umpteenth baco of the night without thinking.
text: It is white rum with cola and a slice of lime. At almost every student party someone is holding a baco. The Dutch love shortening drink names. See also despo and esma.

title: Bak trekken
excerpt: Bak trekken means the same as adten: downing your drink in one go, often as a punishment.
example: "Lost at cards? Then you have to trek a bak," his opponent grinned.
text: You mostly hear it when someone uses an anytimer and you have to finish your drink in one go. In English you would say chug or down it. Going for the fast version? Then grab a straw for a rietadt.

title: Bakken vouwen
excerpt: Bakken vouwen means drinking a lot of beers in a row.
example: At the borrel he was bakken vouwen with his housemates all night.
text: It is often mentioned in the same breath as bak trekken. But bakken vouwen is about how many drinks you have, not how fast you finish one. Only for heavyweights.

title: Bal
excerpt: A bal, or corpsbal, is Dutch student slang for a male member of a traditional corps student association.
example: With his chinos and polo he stood out right away as a typical bal at the party.
text: People also use it more loosely for someone who looks or acts like a typical corps member. Even if they aren't a member at all. Think posh clothes, a loud voice and a lot of confidence.

title: Barco
excerpt: Barco is short for "barcommissie", the bar committee that pours the beers at a Dutch student association.
example: She signed up for the barco right away, because pouring beers sounded amazing.
text: The barco pours and sells drinks during borrels and parties. They often handle the stock for the whole year too. A popular committee. For obvious reasons.

title: Barf
excerpt: Barf means throwing up, usually after drinking too much or too fast.
example: Halfway through the party he suddenly disappeared towards the toilet to barf.
text: It usually happens after a lot of alcohol or mixing different drinks. Eating a proper meal before you start drinking makes it a lot less likely. The Dutch call that bodem leggen.

title: Based
excerpt: Based means someone dares to be themselves or has an honest opinion, even if it isn't popular.
example: "He just ordered a sparkling water while the whole table was drinking beer. Based."
text: Rapper Lil B gave the word this positive meaning around 2010. Based is pretty much the opposite of cringe. You say it as a compliment to someone who doesn't care what others think.

title: Batsen
excerpt: Batsen is Dutch student slang for having sex.
example: After the party she hinted that she had been batsen that night.
text: You mostly hear it in stories about a night out where things went further than just kissing. It is casual and a bit cheeky. Not a word for the family dinner table.

title: Beer pong
excerpt: Beer pong is a drinking game where you throw ping pong balls into cups of beer on the other side of the table.
example: "Us against you, beer pong. Losers buy the next round."
text: You usually play beer pong with two teams. Land a ball in the other team's cup and they drink it. The first team to hit all the cups wins. You see it at almost every house party.

title: Before and after
excerpt: A before and after compares how something looked first with how it looks now.
example: "Check this before and after of our student room. You won't recognise it."
text: You see before and afters online all the time. Make-up, workouts, renovations or a new haircut. They show in one glance how big the change is. A big change for the better is called a glow-up.

title: Beige flag
excerpt: A beige flag is a trait that isn't good or bad. It is just a little weird or boring.
example: "He calls his cat by its full name, surname included. Beige flag."
text: A beige flag sits between a red flag and a green flag. It is no reason to run, but you do notice it. Usually it is about odd habits or boring choices. People mostly say it with a wink.

title: Benching
excerpt: Benching means keeping someone on the hook as a backup, without really going for it.
example: "He only texts me when his other dates fall through. I'm being benched."
text: The word comes from sports, where substitutes sit on the bench. When you get benched you get just enough attention to stay interested. But a real date or relationship never happens.

title: Berig
excerpt: Berig means someone is clearly looking for romantic or sexual contact.
example: He was clearly berig that night, because he talked to everyone at the bar.
text: Berig is about the searching, not the result. So someone who is berig hasn't necessarily been batsen. The closest English word is thirsty.

title: Bestuur
excerpt: The bestuur is the board that runs a Dutch student association.
example: Next year she joins the bestuur as treasurer of the association.
text: Board members run the association for a full year, often while pausing their studies. Committees like the barco help them out. The bestuur also organises the ALV and the constitutieborrel, where a new board is celebrated.

title: Bet
excerpt: Bet means okay, fine or deal. You agree with something.
example: "Shall we meet at the bar at ten?" "Bet."
text: Bet is a short and relaxed yes. It can also be a challenge, like "bet you won't do it". Lose that one and you might owe someone an anytimer. The word comes from African American English.

title: Bij
excerpt: Bij (Dutch for bee) is how Dutch students say they will be there. Often just with a bee emoji.
example: "Bij!" she texted right away when the date for the dinner was set.
text: It is a pun. "Bij" means bee, but "erbij" also means being there. So in a group chat people react with a 🐝 to say they are coming. Everyone sees in one glance who joins.

title: Bits
excerpt: Bits is Dutch slang for something that sucks or is really annoying.
example: "Bits, I just failed my exam," he sighed.
text: You can use it for almost anything. A missed bus. A broken bike. Rain on your way to class. If it is annoying, it is bits.
